headline: High-risk shared filesystem and git state make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write the filesystem, and both support MCP/tool use. Gemini CLI explicitly shares state with other instances via filesystem and git, while Goose shares via filesystem. That creates a default path for one agent to ingest the other’s outputs as trusted file content, enabling instruction hijacking even without a direct chat bridge.
conditions: IF either agent reads the other’s generated files as instructions or prompts
IF both agents operate in the same workspace without isolation
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for each agent
Disable automatic ingestion of peer-generated files
Require manual review before one agent consumes the other’s outputs
Run one agent in a sandboxed container
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for agent-authored files

B_data_leakage.rationale: The pair shares a filesystem/workspace path, and both agents can read files in cwd or the user filesystem. Gemini CLI also handles GEMINI_API_KEY and can call broad network APIs; Goose handles model provider keys and extension tokens. Sensitive files in the shared workspace can therefore flow into either agent’s context and onward to external model providers by default.
conditions: IF secrets or regulated files are present in the shared workspace
IF either agent is allowed to send file contents to its backend or configured providers
mitigations: Move secrets out of the shared workspace
Restrict both agents to a scrubbed project directory
Rotate any exposed API keys after shared-workspace use
Disable file attachment or auto-context features where available
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent secret redaction before upload

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, subprocess spawning, package installation, and git-state modification. Gemini CLI says shared state with other instances is via filesystem and git; Goose shares via filesystem. Concurrent edits to the same repo or working tree can overwrite each other or corrupt git state, and no locking mechanism is documented in either profile.
conditions: IF both agents modify the same repository or directory concurrently
IF git operations occur without external locking or coordination
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout
Serialize git writes with a lock file
Pause one agent before the other commits
Use read-only mode for one agent during analysis
requires-engineering: add transactional workspace coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: Both agents can produce and consume files in the same workspace, and both have tool-using coding-agent behavior. If one agent’s output is treated as authoritative by the other, errors can cascade into edits, package installs, or git commits. The profiles do not show a verification barrier between agents, so the safer choice is high rather than medium.
conditions: IF one agent consumes the other agent’s generated plan, patch, or summary without independent verification
IF downstream actions such as shell commands or git commits are taken from that output
mitigations: Require a human review step between agents
Have the second agent re-derive critical facts independently
Limit one agent to drafting only
Disable auto-apply of patches from peer output
requires-engineering: add structured verification and provenance checks

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source coding agents with docs-only evidence and no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented. The main compliance concern is indirect: Gemini CLI handles Google account login optionally and API keys, while Goose handles provider and extension tokens. Without a documented mismatch, only a low residual compliance risk is supported.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into either agent without a matching policy review
IF an operator configures a provider or extension with stricter residency or retention rules than the workspace
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both agents
Review provider retention settings before use
Document which secrets each agent may access
Use separate accounts for each agent
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data classes
